extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and participants in PTAB post-grant review (attorneys, examiners, parties, and judges)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria used by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board to evaluate indefiniteness and obviousness (Graham/KSR framework) in a post-grant review of a percussive massager patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court’s test for words of degree (e.g., 'substantially')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Words of degree like "substantially" are not "inherently indefinite," but "the court must determine whether the patent provides some standard for measuring that degree."' (quoting Biosig Instruments, Inc. v. Nautilus, Inc., 783 F.3d 1374, 1378 (Fed. Cir. 2015)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for whether the specification supplies a standard or examples that would allow a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) to measure the degree. Practical/functional standards (e.g., 'sufficiently cylindrical to enable attachment while piston reciprocates') can satisfy this test. Anti-pattern: declaring a term definite without showing any guiding examples or function in the intrinsic record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness — intrinsic evidence must provide guidelines/examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the intrinsic evidence provides a general guideline and examples sufficient to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to determine the scope of the claims, the claims are not indefinite even though the construction defines the term without reference to a precise numerical measurement. (Enzo Biochem, Inc. v. Applera Corp., 599 F.3d 1325, 1335 (Fed. Cir. 2010)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the specification and figures supply enough conceptual guidance (examples, functions, or context) so a POSITA can ascertain claim bounds. Anti-pattern: relying only on extrinsic evidence or numerical thresholds when the intrinsic record lacks any guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness — proper focus of the test
rubrics_metrics.description: The test for indefiniteness does not depend on a potential infringer's ability to ascertain the nature of its own accused product to determine infringement, but instead on whether the claim delineates to a skilled artisan the bounds of the invention. (SmithKline Beecham Corp. v. Apotex Corp., 403 F.3d 1331, 1340–41 (Fed. Cir. 2005)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claim clarity from the viewpoint of a POSITA at the time of invention using intrinsic evidence (and permissible extrinsic evidence), not from the accused infringer's perspective. Anti-pattern: measuring definiteness by whether an accused product can be easily tested against the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The four Graham factual inquiries: (1) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (2) ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) considering objective evidence indicating obviousness or non-obviousness. (Graham v. John Deere, cited; summarized in KSR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure obviousness analysis around these four factors. Collect and analyze prior-art disclosures, map claim limitations to references, articulate POSITA qualifications, and assemble/assess secondary considerations (objective indicia) if present. Scoring note: omission of any Graham factor undermines a complete legal analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR principle — predictable combination is likely obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: "The combination of familiar elements according to known methods is likely to be obvious when it does no more than yield predictable results." (KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398 (2007)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claimed combination merely uses prior-art elements in their established functions to achieve predictable results, that combination tends toward obviousness. Emphasize whether the claimed improvement is more than the predictable use of prior-art elements. Anti-pattern: treating mere novelty of combination as sufficient without showing non‑predictability or synergistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation-to-combine — flexible, context-dependent analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The motivation-to-combine analysis is a flexible one: '[a]ny need or problem known in the field of endeavor at the time of invention and addressed by the patent can provide a reason for combining the elements in the manner claimed,' and the analysis 'need not seek out precise teachings directed to the specific subject matter of the challenged claim, for a court can take account of the inferences and creative steps that a person of ordinary skill in the art would employ.' (quoting KSR; Intel Corp. v. PACT XXP Schweiz AG, 61 F.4th 1373, 1379–80 (Fed. Cir. 2023)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for general field problems, known techniques, or commonly-used design choices that would lead a POSITA to combine references. Evidence of generalizability, analogies, or common design tradeoffs supports motivation. Anti-pattern: treating 'motivation' as requiring an explicit sentence in a reference saying "combine this with that."

rubrics_metrics.name: Known technique transferability — expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If a technique has been used to improve one device [or method], and a person of ordinary skill in the art would recognize that it would improve similar devices [or methods] in the same way, using the technique is obvious unless its actual application is beyond his or her skill.' (quoting KSR and Intel/Qualcomm decisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the technique from one reference would be recognized by a POSITA as applicable to the other device, and whether there would be a reasonable expectation of success. Consider compatibility (e.g., similar motors/drive systems) and whether implementation would require routine engineering versus inventive skill. Anti-pattern: assuming transferability when the two systems are incompatible or would require significant redesign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability standard for choosing prior-art combination
rubrics_metrics.description: If addressing a known problem, the prior art combination need not be 'the best option, only . . . a suitable option.' (Intel Corp. v. PACT XXP Schweiz AG quoting KSR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A POSITA need only have a reasonable basis to select a suitable prior-art combination that would solve the problem; perfection or optimality is not required to show obviousness. Anti-pattern: demanding that the cited references be the optimal or sole solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and argument weight — unsworn attorney statements are not evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: '[U]nsworn attorney argument . . . is not evidence.' (Icon Health & Fitness, Inc. v. Strava, Inc., 849 F.3d 1034, 1043 (Fed. Cir. 2017)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support factual assertions with admissible evidence (expert declarations, prior-art documents, prosecution history). Do not rely solely on counsel argument; mark and verify evidence (e.g., sworn declarations) where factual disputes exist. Anti-pattern: using counsel argument as substitute for evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obviousness cannot be shown by attacking references individually
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Non-obviousness cannot be established by attacking references individually where the rejection is based upon the teachings of a combination of references.' (In re Merck & Co., 800 F.2d 1091, 1097 (Fed. Cir. 1986)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the rejection/claim construction is based on a combination of references, responding parties must address the combination as a whole rather than merely pointing out defects in each reference standing alone. Anti-pattern: failing to explain why the combination itself would not have been made or would have failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prosecution history and figures as intrinsic interpretive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence such as patent figures and prosecution statements can exemplify and clarify claim scope (e.g., figures exemplifying cylindrical pockets; prosecution arguments distinguishing references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider drawings, specification passages, and arguments made during prosecution to construe claim terms and to understand what a POSITA would have understood. Use prosecution history to interpret why applicants distinguished prior art, but treat attorney statements in prosecution cautiously if unsworn. Anti-pattern: ignoring intrinsic evidence in favor of post hoc interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional sufficiency for claim limitations (example: 'substantially cylindrical')
rubrics_metrics.description: A functional/operational test can define a 'degree' term: e.g., the pocket 'needs to be sufficiently cylindrical to enable the massaging head to be attached while the massage device’s piston is reciprocating. If the massaging head can be attached while the massage device’s piston is reciprocating, the pocket is substantially cylindrical.' (Patent Owner's asserted functional standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional tests tied to the invention's operation can supply sufficient guidance to a POSITA to make a degree term definite. Evaluate whether the functionality described in the specification or prior art provides an operative standard. Anti-pattern: defining degree terms in purely subjective or aspirational language with no operational anchor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional configuration sufficiency for claim elements (example: 'quick release connector configured to secure while reciprocating')
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior-art language such as 'changing of the patter assembly ... can be easily accomplished ... automatically disconnected merely by turning each other' can be reasonably understood to satisfy a claim recitation of a 'quick release connector' that secures a massaging head while the piston reciprocates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a prior-art disclosure meets a functional claim limitation, consider whether the prior art's description and figures show that the structure is configured to perform the claimed function (e.g., secure during reciprocation and permit quick removal). Anti-pattern: requiring an explicit label 'quick release' in the reference when the functional behavior is disclosed.
